evals.prompt: /review-deps Can you check if our npm dependencies have any known vulnerabilities?
assertions: Detects package.json/package-lock.json and runs an npm audit command (npm audit --json or npm audit)
Cites specific package names, versions, and CVE/GHSA IDs from actual audit tool output, not invented ones

Performs the vulnerability/license/staleness analysis itself sequentially in one pass rather than spawning 3 parallel Explore agents for a single small npm project (fan-out is reserved for unusually large audit output)
Does not modify package.json, package-lock.json, or run npm install/npm audit fix
Produces a report with risk levels (Critical/High/Medium/Low) backed by evidence from the audit output

evals.prompt: /review-deps We're about to go closed-source, please check our dependencies for any copyleft or risky licenses only
assertions: Scopes the audit to license compliance only, skipping vulnerability and staleness phases per the Scoping rule
Reads manifest/lock files to identify actual license fields rather than guessing licenses
Flags copyleft licenses (e.g. GPL, AGPL) as High/Critical risk for a proprietary/closed-source project
Does not run npm audit or cargo audit commands since only license analysis was requested
Report references the actual license field from the package manifest for each flagged package

evals.prompt: /review-deps Our monorepo has a Node service and a Python service, tell me which dependencies are outdated or abandoned and what's the risk of upgrading
assertions: Detects both package managers (package.json/lock for Node, pyproject.toml/requirements for Python) via manifest discovery
Runs native audit/version-check commands appropriate to each ecosystem (e.g. npm audit and pip-audit) in parallel

Assesses staleness with current version, latest version, and upgrade breaking-change complexity per package, either sequentially or via parallel per-dimension agents given the two-ecosystem output size — either is acceptable as long as both ecosystems are actually covered
Never proposes or executes an actual upgrade/install command — recommendations only, no lock-file changes
Cross-references findings across the two ecosystems in a single consolidated report with prioritized actions

evals.prompt: /review-deps Check our Python dependencies for vulnerabilities — heads up, I don't think pip-audit is installed in this environment
assertions: Attempts the pip-audit command (or the pip/uv fallback) and observes it is unavailable rather than assuming without trying
Does not run any command to install pip-audit or any other missing audit tool, and does not install/upgrade/modify any project dependency
Does not fabricate a CVE ID, vulnerable package, or version number to fill the gap left by the missing tool

The report explicitly marks the Python ecosystem's vulnerability audit as not run / tool unavailable (e.g. in the Audit Tool Output Summary) rather than presenting a report that reads as a complete clean scan
Recommends installing pip-audit as a follow-up step without executing that install itself, and stops there instead of guessing at risk
